clinicalPearls: Caused by muscarine-containing mushrooms, chiefly Inocybe and Clitocybe species, and produces a pure cholinergic (muscarinic) toxidrome.
Onset is rapid, typically within a short time of ingestion, distinguishing it from the dangerous delayed-onset amatoxin and gyromitrin poisonings.

Features follow the SLUDGE pattern: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defaecation, gastrointestinal cramping and emesis, together with sweating, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, miosis, blurred vision and bradycardia.
Muscarine directly stimulates peripheral muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and, unlike acetylcholine, is not degraded by acetylcholinesterase, so effects are sustained.

Because muscarine is a quaternary amine it does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so central nervous system effects are absent, in contrast to the delirium of Amanita muscaria (which paradoxically contains little muscarine).
Atropine is the specific antidote, titrated against secretions and bradycardia rather than pupil size.
Profuse secretions and bronchorrhoea, not bronchospasm alone, are the main threat to the airway and gas exchange in severe cases.
Illness is usually self-limiting over hours, and full recovery is the rule with prompt supportive care and antimuscarinic therapy where needed.
reference.pathophysiology: Muscarine poisoning follows ingestion of mushrooms rich in muscarine, a quaternary ammonium alkaloid found in high concentration in many Inocybe and Clitocybe species. Muscarine is a direct agonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors on the effector organs of the parasympathetic nervous system and on sweat glands. Because it is structurally resistant to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase, its receptor stimulation is prolonged compared with endogenous acetylcholine. Activation of these receptors increases exocrine secretion (salivary, lacrimal, sweat and bronchial glands), stimulates smooth muscle of the gut and bronchi, contracts the detrusor and pupillary sphincter, and slows the heart through vagal effects on the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. The resulting clinical picture is the classic muscarinic toxidrome. Crucially, the fixed positive charge of the quaternary amine prevents muscarine from crossing the blood-brain barrier, so central effects such as agitation and hallucination are absent; this pharmacology also explains why the antidote atropine, a tertiary amine that does cross into the central nervous system, effectively blocks the peripheral receptors.
additionalDifferentials: Amanita muscaria/pantherina (ibotenic acid and muscimol) poisoning with central features
Cholinergic effects of medicinal cholinesterase inhibitors
Acute asthma or other cause of bronchospasm
Vasovagal episode causing bradycardia and sweating
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of the cholinergic toxidrome including heart rate, secretions and pupils
Electrocardiogram and continuous cardiac monitoring for bradyarrhythmias
Pulse oximetry and respiratory assessment for bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm
Serum electrolytes and renal function given fluid losses from secretions and diarrhoea
Red cell and plasma cholinesterase activity to help exclude organophosphate poisoning
Blood glucose and basic metabolic screen to exclude mimics
Mycological identification of the ingested mushrooms
redFlags: Copious bronchial secretions or bronchorrhoea threatening the airway
Marked volume depletion from combined secretory losses
Uncertainty distinguishing it from organophosphate poisoning
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; symptoms are usually self-limiting over several hours and recovery is complete, with deaths being very rare when supportive care and atropine are available. Severe cases are typically those with delayed treatment of profuse secretions and bradycardia.
pitfalls: Assuming Amanita muscaria is the culprit for muscarinic symptoms, when Inocybe and Clitocybe are the usual high-muscarine sources
Titrating atropine to pupil size rather than to drying of secretions and heart rate
Missing coexisting organophosphate poisoning that produces an identical peripheral picture
Underestimating fluid loss from combined salivation, sweating, vomiting and diarrhoea
Expecting central nervous system features, whose absence is characteristic of pure muscarine poisoning
references: Mushroom poisoning and poisons-centre reference materials
